segments.say: There's a last thing to look at, and it turns the whole question around. So far we've asked about the people doing the judging. Now let's ask about the person being judged.

Felix remembers something that made him wince a little this morning. On the studio's website, there's a staff page, and he's already on it. His photograph was taken in a hurry, three weeks ago, in a corridor, by a friend with a phone. In it, he looks slightly startled, as though someone has just said his name from behind. It isn't how he feels. It isn't even how he usually looks.

And he wonders what impression that photograph gives to a stranger who sees it for a tenth of a second. Startled? Nervous? Odd? It's an uncomfortable thought, and it leads straight to the last of the studies, which asked exactly that. How much does a single photograph of a person really tell you about the person?

In 2014, Todorov and Porter published a paper in the journal Psychological Science, with a title that says it all. Misleading first impressions, different for different facial images of the same person. They collected several straight-on headshots of the same people, taken in comparable lighting, and asked people to rate them on traits such as attractiveness, competence, trustworthiness and intelligence.

show.what: People rated different straight-on headshots of the same individuals, taken under comparable lighting, on traits such as attractiveness, competence, trustworthiness and intelligence.

segments.say: The photographs differed only in the small ways that any two photographs of one person differ. A slightly different expression. A different moment. A tilt of the head. The kind of variation you'd get from taking a few pictures in a row, which is exactly what happens every time anyone takes a photograph.

And here's what they found. The ratings of one person's photographs varied about as much as ratings of different people. In other words, the difference between two photos of the same person was about as large as the difference between two different people. A face, on its own, is surprisingly unstable as a source of information about the person.

show.text: Ratings varied as much across photos of one person as across different people.

segments.say: People also had views about which photograph was best for which purpose. For an online dating profile, they preferred certain photographs. For an audition for a movie villain, others. For a political campaign, yet others. And those preferences appeared even when the photographs were shown for only a fraction of a second.

It's a gentle but important finding. The impression you get from a photograph is an impression of the photograph. The person in it is richer, odder and more variable than any one frame. The researcher Todorov was quoted as saying that impressions from still photographs of individuals could be deeply misleading. And it's a surprisingly comforting thought for anyone who has ever hated a picture of themselves.

show.sub: Not the same as the person

segments.say: Here's a quiet picture to hold. A garden bench, seen on a sunny morning, and again on a rainy afternoon, and again at dusk. It's the same bench. But in each light, it looks like a different place. A single photograph of a person is a bit like one of those moments.

So, the last question. If a first impression has been formed, and it's imperfect, does it stick? Do we revise it when we meet the person? A study published in 2017 by Gul Gunaydin, Emre Selcuk and Vivian Zayas asked that, and the way they did it was rather lovely.

Fifty-five people first rated photographs of four women, on likeability and on five personality traits. Then, one to six months later, they came to the lab and, without knowing it, met one of the women they'd rated. They played a ten-minute trivia game with her, chatted for ten minutes, and rated her again, now that they really knew something about her.

show.what: Fifty-five people rated photographs of four women, and one to six months later met one of them, played a 10-minute trivia game, chatted for 10 minutes, and rated her again.

segments.say: And here's what they found. Impressions based on the photograph strongly matched impressions after the live meeting. If someone liked the photograph, they tended to like the woman. If they disliked it, they tended not to. The researchers also noted that people who had liked the photograph tended to act warmer and more engaged during the meeting, which might well have drawn warmth back from her.

That's a delicate and important point. A first impression doesn't only colour how we see someone. It can also shape how we behave toward them, and the way we behave can shape how they behave toward us. A warm impression can invite warmth back. A cool one can invite cool. The impression can end up creating some of its own evidence.

There was a related finding in the same paper. In a companion study, people said they would revise their judgments after meeting someone, but the data showed very little actual revision. So we tend to believe we'll update, and we tend to update less than we expect. Not out of stubbornness, but because the impression is quietly steering the meeting.

show.cap: People expect to change their minds

segments.say: But there's real good news, too. In 2019, a group of researchers including Ferguson reviewed work on when the quick, automatic kind of impression can be updated. They found that it can change, and quite quickly, under three kinds of conditions. When new information is highly diagnostic, when it is highly believable, or when it reframes earlier experiences.

Notice what those three have in common. In each case, the new information is clear. It isn't just more of the same, and it isn't vague. A single, believable fact that really settles something can move an impression a long way. And a fresh way of seeing an old moment can do it, too. Changing a mind seems to be less about quantity, and more about the quality and clarity of the evidence.

So what might Felix do, tomorrow? Nothing dramatic. He doesn't have to decide that Mara is warm. He might simply remember that the word cold arrived before the door did, that a brisk voice isn't a cold heart, and that a kind sentence at three o'clock is also evidence, and a clear one. He might let that sentence move into the middle of the picture.

He might also be curious. He might ask Mara one real question, about the site plans, or about the studio's old projects. He doesn't have to be warm, or impressive. He only has to give his first draft of her a little more to work with. And that's all that tonight's research really asks. Not trust. Not distrust. Just a bit more evidence, kindly gathered.

That might be the gentlest summary of the whole night. A first impression is quick, shared, and often over-weighted. It's a starting place. And the way to treat a starting place is to keep walking, a little curious, and a little patient, and to let the rest of the person arrive.

show.text: Not trust, and not distrust, but a little more evidence, kindly gathered.

segments.say: And one more thought, to close the story. Tomorrow, Mara will have her own second look at Felix, whether she means to or not. He won't be the nervous person in the doorway with the bag. He'll be a colleague, with a name, and a desk, and a plan to ask a question. It's an easy thing to look forward to, that second look from both sides.

For now, the day is done. The verdicts have been looked at, turned over, and put gently back. Felix lifts his lanyard from the chair, hangs it on the hook by the door, and finally changes out of his work clothes. He climbs under the blanket. The room is dim, and the street is quiet, and tonight, nothing at all needs to be decided.

And so, if you're ready, let's let all of that go together, and settle into a long, slow wind-down. You don't have to do anything. You don't have to follow along, or listen closely. Whatever happens, happens.

Take a slow breath in, and let it out for a little longer than you breathed in. Felix does. Somewhere, a clock ticks, steady and unhurried. Everything you've heard tonight has done its work, and now it can rest. Let the day soften, and let the night come all the way in.
